claim: Tgfbr1 is a key regulator of the trunk to tail transition in mammalian embryos.
source: Genetic and molecular data indicate that Tgfbr1 is a key regulator of the trunk to tail transition.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a conclusion from genetic and molecular data.

claim: Tgfbr1 has been shown to control the switch of neuromesodermal competent cells from the epiblast to the chordoneural hinge to generate the tail bud.
source: Tgfbr1 has been shown to control the switch of the neuromesodermal competent cells from the epiblast to the chordoneural hinge to generate the tail bud.
evidence: Referenced as previously established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: In mouse embryos, Tgfbr1 signaling controls the remodeling of the lateral plate mesoderm associated with the trunk to tail transition.
source: We now show that in mouse embryos Tgfbr1 signaling also controls the remodeling of the lateral plate mesoderm (LPM) and of the embryonic endoderm associated with the trunk to tail transition.
evidence: Primary finding stated in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: In mouse embryos, Tgfbr1 signaling controls the remodeling of the embryonic endoderm associated with the trunk to tail transition.
source: We now show that in mouse embryos Tgfbr1 signaling also controls the remodeling of the lateral plate mesoderm (LPM) and of the embryonic endoderm associated with the trunk to tail transition.
evidence: Primary finding stated in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: In the absence of Tgfbr1, the two LPM layers do not converge at the end of the trunk.
source: In the absence of Tgfbr1, the two LPM layers do not converge at the end of the trunk, extending instead as separate layers until the caudal embryonic extremity, and failing to activate markers of primordia for the hindlimb and external genitalia.
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos described in the abstract.

claim: In the absence of Tgfbr1, the LPM layers extend as separate layers until the caudal embryonic extremity.
source: In the absence of Tgfbr1, the two LPM layers do not converge at the end of the trunk, extending instead as separate layers until the caudal embryonic extremity, and failing to activate markers of primordia for the hindlimb and external genitalia.
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos described in the abstract.

claim: In the absence of Tgfbr1, embryos fail to activate markers of primordia for the hindlimb and external genitalia.
source: In the absence of Tgfbr1, the two LPM layers do not converge at the end of the trunk, extending instead as separate layers until the caudal embryonic extremity, and failing to activate markers of primordia for the hindlimb and external genitalia.
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos described in the abstract.

claim: The vascular remodeling involving the dorsal aorta and the umbilical artery leading to the connection between embryonic and extraembryonic circulation was affected in Tgfbr1 mutant embryos.
source: The vascular remodeling involving the dorsal aorta and the umbilical artery leading to the connection between embryonic and extraembryonic circulation was also affected in the Tgfbr1 mutant embryos.
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos described in the abstract.

claim: Similar alterations in the LPM and vascular system were observed in Isl1 null mutants.
source: Similar alterations in the LPM and vascular system were also observed in Isl1 null mutants, indicating that this factor acts in the regulatory cascade downstream of Tgfbr1 in LPM-derived tissues.
evidence: Direct observation from Isl1 mutant embryos described in the abstract.

claim: Isl1 acts in the regulatory cascade downstream of Tgfbr1 in LPM-derived tissues.
source: Similar alterations in the LPM and vascular system were also observed in Isl1 null mutants, indicating that this factor acts in the regulatory cascade downstream of Tgfbr1 in LPM-derived tissues.
evidence: Inference drawn from the similarity of phenotypes between Tgfbr1 and Isl1 mutants.

claim: In the absence of Tgfbr1, the embryonic endoderm fails to expand to form the endodermal cloaca.
source: In addition, in the absence of Tgfbr1 the embryonic endoderm fails to expand to form the endodermal cloaca and to extend posteriorly to generate the tail gut.
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos described in the abstract.

claim: In the absence of Tgfbr1, the embryonic endoderm fails to extend posteriorly to generate the tail gut.
source: In addition, in the absence of Tgfbr1 the embryonic endoderm fails to expand to form the endodermal cloaca and to extend posteriorly to generate the tail gut.
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos described in the abstract.

claim: The remodeling activity of Tgfbr1 in the LPM and endoderm results from the control of the posterior PS fate after its regression during the trunk to tail transition.
source: We present evidence suggesting that the remodeling activity of Tgfbr1 in the LPM and endoderm results from the control of the posterior PS fate after its regression during the trunk to tail transition.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tgfbr1 is at the top of the regulatory processes controlling the trunk to tail transition.
source: Our data, together with previously reported observations, place Tgfbr1 at the top of the regulatory processes controlling the trunk to tail transition.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the current study and previous literature.

claim: Extension through the trunk is driven by axial progenitors located within the epiblast.
source: Extension through the trunk is driven by axial progenitors located within the epiblast, that generate the spinal cord, the embryonic gut, and the different mesodermal compartments (Binagui-Casas et al., 2021; Cambray and Wilson, 2007; Henrique et al., 2015; Steventon and Martinez Arias, 2017; Tsakiridis and Wilson, 2015; Wilson et al., 2009; Wymeersch et al., 2021).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Axial progenitors in the epiblast generate the spinal cord, the embryonic gut, and the different mesodermal compartments.
source: Extension through the trunk is driven by axial progenitors located within the epiblast, that generate the spinal cord, the embryonic gut, and the different mesodermal compartments (Binagui-Casas et al., 2021; Cambray and Wilson, 2007; Henrique et al., 2015; Steventon and Martinez Arias, 2017; Tsakiridis and Wilson, 2015; Wilson et al., 2009; Wymeersch et al., 2021).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The caudal end of the mouse embryo is occupied by the allantois during trunk extension.
source: At this stage, the caudal end of the mouse embryo is occupied by the allantois that will play an essential role in the connection between embryonic and extraembryonic structures (Arora and Papaioannou, 2012; Rodriguez and Downs, 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The allantois plays an essential role in the connection between embryonic and extraembryonic structures.
source: At this stage, the caudal end of the mouse embryo is occupied by the allantois that will play an essential role in the connection between embryonic and extraembryonic structures (Arora and Papaioannou, 2012; Rodriguez and Downs, 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The transition to tail development is associated with the progressive anterior relocation of the allantois along the ventral side of the embryo.
source: The transition to tail development is associated with changes in the global anatomy of the caudal end of the embryo, involving the progressive anterior relocation of the allantois along the ventral side of the embryo.
evidence: Established knowledge about embryonic development.

claim: The tail bud forms at the dorsal and posterior end of the embryo during the trunk to tail transition.
source: During this process, the tail bud forms at the dorsal and posterior end of the embryo, and replaces the epiblast/primitive streak (PS) as the main driver of axial extension (Henrique et al., 2015; Wilson et al., 2009).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The tail bud replaces the epiblast/primitive streak as the main driver of axial extension.
source: During this process, the tail bud forms at the dorsal and posterior end of the embryo, and replaces the epiblast/primitive streak (PS) as the main driver of axial extension (Henrique et al., 2015; Wilson et al., 2009).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Formation of the tail bud results from changes in the neuro-mesodermal-competent population, which relocates from the epiblast to the chordo-neural hinge.
source: Formation of the tail bud results from changes in the progenitors generating the neural and paraxial mesodermal structures, the so-called neuro-mesodermal-competent (NMC) population, which relocates from the epiblast to the chordo-neural hinge (CNH) (Binagui-Casas et al., 2021; Cambray and Wilson, 2007; Wymeersch et al., 2021).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The lateral plate mesoderm is composed of two layers: a ventral splanchnopleure and a lateral somatopleure.
source: This mesodermal compartment, generated by progenitors situated at the caudal region of the epiblast and PS (Wymeersch et al., 2021; Wymeersch et al., 2019; Wymeersch et al., 2016) is composed of two layers: a ventral splanchnopleure, which contributes to the formation of the various body organs, as well as their vascularization, and a lateral somatopleure involved in the formation of the body wall (Prummel et al., 2020).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The splanchnopleure contributes to the formation of various body organs and their vascularization.
source: This mesodermal compartment, generated by progenitors situated at the caudal region of the epiblast and PS (Wymeersch et al., 2021; Wymeersch et al., 2019; Wymeersch et al., 2016) is composed of two layers: a ventral splanchnopleure, which contributes to the formation of the various body organs, as well as their vascularization, and a lateral somatopleure involved in the formation of the body wall (Prummel et al., 2020).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The somatopleure is involved in the formation of the body wall.
source: This mesodermal compartment, generated by progenitors situated at the caudal region of the epiblast and PS (Wymeersch et al., 2021; Wymeersch et al., 2019; Wymeersch et al., 2016) is composed of two layers: a ventral splanchnopleure, which contributes to the formation of the various body organs, as well as their vascularization, and a lateral somatopleure involved in the formation of the body wall (Prummel et al., 2020).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The two LPM layers delimit the celomic cavity, which will hold the animal's internal organs.
source: These two layers delimit the celomic cavity, which will hold the animal's internal organs.
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge.

claim: During allantois relocation, the two LPM layers converge toward the midline, ending the celomic cavity and marking the posterior border of the trunk.
source: During allantois relocation, the two LPM layers converge toward the midline, ending the celomic cavity and marking the posterior border of the trunk.
evidence: Established developmental process.

claim: Remodeling of the caudal part of the embryo is associated with the induction of the hindlimbs from the somatopleure.
source: This remodeling of the caudal part of the embryo is associated with the induction of the hindlimbs from the somatopleure (Tickle, 2015), and the generation of the pericloacal mesenchyme, the primordium of the genital tuberculum (GT) (Cohn, 2011; Yamada et al., 2006), from the ventral lateral mesoderm (VLM) posterior to the allantois (Tschopp et al., 2014).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The pericloacal mesenchyme, the primordium of the genital tuberculum, is generated from the ventral lateral mesoderm posterior to the allantois.
source: This remodeling of the caudal part of the embryo is associated with the induction of the hindlimbs from the somatopleure (Tickle, 2015), and the generation of the pericloacal mesenchyme, the primordium of the genital tuberculum (GT) (Cohn, 2011; Yamada et al., 2006), from the ventral lateral mesoderm (VLM) posterior to the allantois (Tschopp et al., 2014).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: When the allantois relocates, the embryonic endoderm forms a cavity that will originate the cloaca.
source: When the allantois relocates, the embryonic endoderm, whose posterior end reaches the base of the allantois, forms a cavity that will originate the cloaca, an endodermal expansion that becomes the common end of the excretory, intestinal, and genital tracts (Huang et al., 2016; Matsumaru et al., 2015).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The cloaca is an endodermal expansion that becomes the common end of the excretory, intestinal, and genital tracts.
source: When the allantois relocates, the embryonic endoderm, whose posterior end reaches the base of the allantois, forms a cavity that will originate the cloaca, an endodermal expansion that becomes the common end of the excretory, intestinal, and genital tracts (Huang et al., 2016; Matsumaru et al., 2015).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The pronephric ducts, derivatives of the intermediate mesoderm, merge with the cloaca to engage in the development of the urogenital system.
source: The pronephric ducts, derivatives of the intermediate mesoderm (IM) located medially to the splanchnic and somatic LPM layers, later merge with the cloaca to engage in the development of the urogenital system (Davidson, 2008).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In the mouse embryo, the embryonic endoderm expands caudally to generate the tail gut, a transient structure with unknown function.
source: In the mouse embryo, the embryonic endoderm then expands further caudally to generate the tail gut, a transient structure with unknown function.
evidence: Established anatomical observation.

claim: The region of the posterior visceral endoderm abutting the allantois is thought to facilitate the invagination and growth of the embryonic endoderm.
source: The region of the posterior visceral (extraembryonic) endoderm abutting the allantois is thought to facilitate the invagination and growth of the embryonic endoderm (Rodriguez and Downs, 2017) and contribute to the hindgut epithelium (Kwon et al., 2008; Nowotschin et al., 2019).
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: The posterior visceral endoderm contributes to the hindgut epithelium.
source: The region of the posterior visceral (extraembryonic) endoderm abutting the allantois is thought to facilitate the invagination and growth of the embryonic endoderm (Rodriguez and Downs, 2017) and contribute to the hindgut epithelium (Kwon et al., 2008; Nowotschin et al., 2019).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The caudal end of the paired dorsal aortae merge and connect with the umbilical artery generated within the allantois.
source: The caudal end of the paired dorsal aortae (DA) merge and connect with the umbilical artery generated within the allantois (Arora and Papaioannou, 2012; Downs and Rodriguez, 2020).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: As the allantois moves forward, the caudal end of the DA bends to form the recurved dorsal aorta.
source: As the allantois move forward, the caudal end of the DA bends to form the recurved dorsal aorta (rDA).
evidence: Established developmental process.

claim: Formation of the recurved dorsal aorta requires the generation of a vessel of confluence from the caudal end of the PS abutting the allantois.
source: It is thought that this process requires the generation of a vessel of confluence from the caudal end of the PS abutting the allantois, which will constitute a major part of the rDA (Downs and Rodriguez, 2020; Rodriguez and Downs, 2017).
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: Gdf11 signaling is an integral component of the gene regulatory network controlling the trunk to tail transition.
source: Molecular and genetic data indicate that Gdf11 signaling is an integral component of the gene regulatory network controlling the trunk to tail transition (Aires et al., 2019; Jurberg et al., 2013; Matsubara et al., 2017; McPherron et al., 2009; McPherron et al., 1999).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Gdf11 activity is predominantly mediated by transforming growth factor β receptor 1 (Tgfbr1).
source: Gdf11 activity is predominantly mediated by transforming grow factorβ receptor 1 (Tgfbr1) (also known as Alk5) (Andersson et al., 2006).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Premature expression of a constitutively active form of Tgfbr1 promotes early execution of the trunk to tail transition program.
source: Indeed, premature expression of a constitutively active form of Tgfbr1 promotes early execution of the trunk to tail transition program (Jurberg et al., 2013).
evidence: Experimental finding supported by citation.

claim: Tgfbr1 is required to trigger formation of the tail bud by promoting, together with Snai1, an incomplete epithelial-to-mesenchymal transformation in the NMC population within the epiblast.
source: In addition, Tgfbr1 is required to trigger formation of the tail bud by promoting, together with Snai1, an incomplete epithelial-to-mesenchymal transformation (EMT) in the NMC population within the epiblast (Dias et al., 2020).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In Tgfbr1 null mutants, the LPM fails to converge leading to the posterior extension of the celomic cavity.
source: In the present study, we show that, in addition to the lack of molecular signals for the induction of the hindlimbs and the GT, the LPM of Tgfbr1 null mutants fail to converge leading to the posterior extension of the celomic cavity.
evidence: Primary finding from the current study.

claim: Tgfbr1 mutants fail to generate a cloacal cavity.
source: In addition, the mutants fail to generate a cloacal cavity and to extend the endodermal tube to form the tail gut.
evidence: Primary finding from the current study.

claim: Tgfbr1 mutants fail to extend the endodermal tube to form the tail gut.
source: In addition, the mutants fail to generate a cloacal cavity and to extend the endodermal tube to form the tail gut.
evidence: Primary finding from the current study.

claim: In Tgfbr1 mutants, the connection between the embryonic and extraembryonic vascular systems fails to undergo normal reorganization, resulting in the expansion of the paired dorsal aorta to reach the caudal end of the embryo.
source: Also, the connection between the embryonic and extraembryonic vascular systems fails to undergo normal reorganization, resulting in the expansion of the paired dorsal aorta to reach the caudal end of the embryo.
evidence: Primary finding from the current study.

claim: Isl1 is the key functional downstream target of Tgfbr1 for the reorganization of the LPM and vascular tissues during the trunk to tail transition.
source: We also provide evidence indicating that Isl1 is the key functional downstream target of Tgfbr1 for the reorganization of the LPM and vascular tissues during the trunk to tail transition, acting on the posterior PS/allantois.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in the current study.

claim: Isl1 acts on the posterior PS/allantois during the trunk to tail transition.
source: We also provide evidence indicating that Isl1 is the key functional downstream target of Tgfbr1 for the reorganization of the LPM and vascular tissues during the trunk to tail transition, acting on the posterior PS/allantois.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in the current study.

claim: Isl1 controls PS fate during its regression.
source: Isl1 controls PS fate during its regression and regulates the establishment of the embryonic–extraembryonic connection during the ventral relocation of the allantois.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in the current study.

claim: Isl1 regulates the establishment of the embryonic–extraembryonic connection during the ventral relocation of the allantois.
source: Isl1 controls PS fate during its regression and regulates the establishment of the embryonic–extraembryonic connection during the ventral relocation of the allantois.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in the current study.

claim: In wild-type embryos, the somatic and splanchnic LPM layers converge at the posterior region of the trunk at both sides of the developing endoderm at E9.5, ending the celomic cavity.
source: In wild-type embryos, the somatic and splanchnic LPM layers converge at the posterior region of the trunk at both sides of the developing endoderm at E9.5, ending the celomic cavity.
evidence: Direct observation from wild-type embryos.

claim: In Tgfbr1 mutant embryos, the two LPM layers and the coelomic cavity continue extending from the trunk region of the embryo until its posterior end.
source: In Tgfbr1 mutant embryos, however, the two LPM layers, and, consequently, the coelomic cavity, continued extending from the trunk region of the embryo until its posterior end (Figure 1b', d').
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 1.

claim: Irx3 is a somatic LPM marker.
source: This was best illustrated by the expression of Irx3 and Foxf1, somatic and splanchnic LPM markers, respectively (Funayama et al., 1999; Mahlapuu et al., 2001).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Foxf1 is a splanchnic LPM marker.
source: This was best illustrated by the expression of Irx3 and Foxf1, somatic and splanchnic LPM markers, respectively (Funayama et al., 1999; Mahlapuu et al., 2001).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Both Irx3 and Foxf1 were expressed following normal patterns in the trunk of Tgfbr1−/− embryos.
source: Both markers were expressed following normal patterns in the trunk of Tgfbr1−/− embryos (Figure 1Aa, Bb, Cc, Dd).
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 1.

claim: In Tgfbr1 null mutant embryos, Irx3 and Foxf1 were not downregulated at the level of the trunk to tail transition.
source: However, in contrast to wild-type controls, in Tgfbr1 null mutant embryos these markers were not downregulated at the level of the trunk to tail transition, being Foxf1 even clearly upregulated in this embryonic region (Figure 1B, D).
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 1.

claim: Foxf1 was clearly upregulated in the trunk to tail transition region of Tgfbr1 null mutant embryos.
source: However, in contrast to wild-type controls, in Tgfbr1 null mutant embryos these markers were not downregulated at the level of the trunk to tail transition, being Foxf1 even clearly upregulated in this embryonic region (Figure 1B, D).
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 1.

claim: In Tgfbr1 null mutant embryos, Irx3 and Foxf1 expression expanded to encompass the entire mesodermal tissue surrounding the celomic cavity.
source: In addition, their expression was no longer restricted to their respective LPM layers, and instead expanded to encompass the entire mesodermal tissue surrounding the celomic cavity.
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos.

claim: In Tgfbr1 mutants, the pronephric ducts extended into the posterior end of the embryo instead of merging with the cloaca.
source: The expression pattern of the IM marker Pax2 at E10.5 revealed that the pronephric ducts also extended into the posterior end of the embryo instead of merging with the cloaca (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, c' , d").
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pronephric ducts were bifurcated in the posterior embryonic end in some Tgfbr1 mutant embryos (2/4).
source: Furthermore, pronephric ducts were bifurcated in the posterior embryonic end in some mutant embryos (2/4) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-d").
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The four orifices surrounding the hindgut in E9.5 embryos observed in transverse sections are diagnostic of the rDA.
source: The four orifices surrounding the hindgut in E9.5 embryos observed in transverse sections, and diagnostic of the rDA (Zakin et al., 2005), were not detected in Tgfbr1 mutants, in which only a single expanded vessel was visible on each side of the gut tube (Figure 1Aa', Bb', Cc', Dd').
evidence: Established anatomical marker supported by citation.

claim: The four orifices diagnostic of the rDA were not detected in Tgfbr1 mutants; instead, only a single expanded vessel was visible on each side of the gut tube.
source: The four orifices surrounding the hindgut in E9.5 embryos observed in transverse sections, and diagnostic of the rDA (Zakin et al., 2005), were not detected in Tgfbr1 mutants, in which only a single expanded vessel was visible on each side of the gut tube (Figure 1Aa', Bb', Cc', Dd').
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 1.

claim: The DA of Tgfbr1 mutant embryos was elongated posteriorly, reaching the tip of the gut tube.
source: Pecam1-aided 3D reconstruction of the main blood vessels revealed that the DA of Tgfbr1 mutant embryos was elongated posteriorly, reaching the tip of the gut tube.
evidence: Direct observation from 3D reconstruction of Tgfbr1 mutant embryos.

claim: The posterior portion of the DA in Tgfbr1 mutants formed a vessel of enlarged diameter.
source: The posterior portion of the DA formed a vessel of enlarged diameter, as observed in the histological sections, that contrasts with the curvature characteristic of the rDA of wild-type embryos (Figure 2).
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 2.

claim: The DA of Tgfbr1 mutants still merged with the umbilical artery, although following patterns different to those observed in control embryos.
source: The DA of the Tgfbr1 mutants still merged with the umbilical artery, although following patterns different to those observed in control embryos.
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos.

claim: In wild-type embryos, the paired rDAs remain as two independent vessels, merging just before their connection with the umbilical artery.
source: For instance, while in wild-type embryos the paired rDAs remained as two independent vessels, merging just before their connection with the umbilical artery (Figure 2b), the two paired arteries of Tgfbr1−/− embryos were fused along most of their path ventral to the endodermal tube, from the posterior embryonic tip to the umbilical artery.
evidence: Direct observation from wild-type embryos shown in Figure 2.

claim: The two paired arteries of Tgfbr1−/− embryos were fused along most of their path ventral to the endodermal tube, from the posterior embryonic tip to the umbilical artery.
source: For instance, while in wild-type embryos the paired rDAs remained as two independent vessels, merging just before their connection with the umbilical artery (Figure 2b), the two paired arteries of Tgfbr1−/− embryos were fused along most of their path ventral to the endodermal tube, from the posterior embryonic tip to the umbilical artery.
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos.

claim: In Tgfbr1 mutants, the allantois appeared to protrude perpendicularly to the embryo instead of following its curvature, as observed in wild-type embryos.
source: In addition, the allantois appeared to protrude perpendicularly to the embryo instead of following its curvature, as observed in wild-type embryos (Figure 2d).
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 2.

claim: Splanchnic Foxf1 expression depends on endodermal Shh activity.
source: Splanchnic Foxf1 expression depends on endodermal Shh activity (Astorga and Carlsson, 2007; Tsiairis and McMahon, 2009).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Foxf1 expression observed in the lateral layer of the expanded LPM of Tgfbr1 mutant embryos is separated from the endoderm by the celomic cavity, suggesting that it is likely to have a Shh-independent origin.
source: The Foxf1 expression observed in the lateral layer of the expanded LPM of Tgfbr1 mutant embryos is separated from the endoderm by the celomic cavity, suggesting that it is likely to have a Shh-independent origin.
evidence: Inference drawn from anatomical observation in Tgfbr1 mutants.

claim: Foxf1 expression has been detected in the posterior PS/allantois of E8.5 embryos.
source: Such Foxf1 expression has been detected in the posterior PS/allantois of E8.5 embryos (Astorga and Carlsson, 2007; Tsiairis and McMahon, 2009), where it plays a role in vasculogenesis (Astorga and Carlsson, 2007).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Foxf1 plays a role in vasculogenesis in the posterior PS/allantois.
source: Such Foxf1 expression has been detected in the posterior PS/allantois of E8.5 embryos (Astorga and Carlsson, 2007; Tsiairis and McMahon, 2009), where it plays a role in vasculogenesis (Astorga and Carlsson, 2007).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Foxf1 expression in the VLM is likely to derive from its expression domain in the posterior PS/allantois.
source: From a functional perspective, Foxf1 expression in the VLM is likely to derive from its expression domain in the posterior PS/allantois (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inference supported by expression pattern shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Foxf1 expression in the posterior PS/allantois is not affected by the absence of Tgfbr1.
source: Foxf1 expression in the posterior PS/allantois is not affected by the absence of Tgfbr1 (Figure 3A, B), consistent with the apparent dispensability of Tgfbr1 activity in axial tissues before the transition to tail development.
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Foxf1-positive cells in the extended LPM of Tgfbr1−/− embryos might represent the derivatives of posterior PS/allantois cells that failed to enter their normal fates.
source: Given the absence of VLM in Tgfbr1−/− embryos, the Foxf1-positive cells in the extended LPM might represent the derivatives of posterior PS/allantois cells that failed to enter their normal fates, which instead become intermingled with LPM cells extending from the trunk.
evidence: Hypothesis based on observations in Tgfbr1 mutants.

claim: The abnormal development of the posterior aortae in Tgfbr1 mutant embryos might result from compromised development of the Foxf1-positive posterior PS/allantois.
source: Indeed, the abnormal development of the posterior aortae in Tgfbr1 mutant embryos might result from compromised development of the Foxf1-positive posterior PS/allantois.
evidence: Hypothesis based on observations in Tgfbr1 mutants.

claim: Tamoxifen administration at E8.0 in T-str-creERT transgenics resulted in labeling of the VLM of E9.5 embryos.
source: Tamoxifen administration at E8.0, which activates cre activity within the 10–12 hr corresponding to E8.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), thus coincident with the start of the trunk to tail transition, resulted in labeling of the VLM of E9.5 embryos, and of the pericloacal mesoderm at E10.0 (Figure 3c).
evidence: Direct observation from lineage tracing experiment shown in Figure 3.

claim: Tamoxifen administration at E8.0 in T-str-creERT transgenics resulted in labeling of the pericloacal mesoderm at E10.0.
source: Tamoxifen administration at E8.0, which activates cre activity within the 10–12 hr corresponding to E8.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), thus coincident with the start of the trunk to tail transition, resulted in labeling of the VLM of E9.5 embryos, and of the pericloacal mesoderm at E10.0 (Figure 3c).
evidence: Direct observation from lineage tracing experiment shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Foxf1-positive posterior PS/allantois is a functional target of Tgfbr1 activity in the LPM during the trunk to tail transition.
source: Although this experiment does not allow regional sub localization within the PS, it is consistent with the Foxf1-positive posterior PS/allantois being a functional target of Tgfbr1 activity in the LPM during the trunk to tail transition.
evidence: Inference drawn from lineage tracing and expression data.

claim: Reporter, gain and loss of function experiments suggested that Isl1 might be functioning downstream of Tgfbr1 signaling in the LPM during the trunk to tail transition.
source: Reporter, gain and loss of function experiments suggested that Isl1 might be functioning downstream of Tgfbr1 signaling in the LPM during the trunk to tail transition (Dias et al., 2020; Jurberg et al., 2013).
evidence: Hypothesis supported by previous studies cited.

claim: Isl1 first becomes activated in axial tissues at the PS/allantois junction, just prior to the transition to tail development.
source: It has been shown that Isl1 first becomes activated in axial tissues at the PS/allantois junction, just prior to the transition to tail development (Cai et al., 2003; Wymeersch et al., 2019), and Isl1-positive cells later contribute to the VLM, the hindlimbs and GT (Yang et al., 2006).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Isl1-positive cells contribute to the VLM, the hindlimbs and GT.
source: It has been shown that Isl1 first becomes activated in axial tissues at the PS/allantois junction, just prior to the transition to tail development (Cai et al., 2003; Wymeersch et al., 2019), and Isl1-positive cells later contribute to the VLM, the hindlimbs and GT (Yang et al., 2006).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Isl1 null embryos were embryonic lethal between E9.5 and E10.5.
source: Isl1 null embryos were embryonic lethal between E9.5 and E10.5, showing malformations in different embryonic structures.
evidence: Direct observation from Isl1 mutant embryos.

claim: Isl1 mutants halted their growth around the stage of the trunk to tail transition, as estimated by the number of somites generated.
source: Regarding axial development, Isl1 mutants halted their growth around the stage of the trunk to tail transition, as estimated by the number of somites generated (Figure 4D–F, I, J), thus reminiscent of the Tgfbr1 mutant phenotype.
evidence: Direct observation from Isl1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 4.

claim: In contrast to Tgfbr1 mutants, Isl1 mutants generated a structure resembling the tail bud which expressed Sox2 and Tbxt in domains comparable to wild-type embryos.
source: However, in contrast to Tgfbr1 mutants, Isl1 mutants generated a structure resembling the tail bud which expressed Sox2 and Tbxt in domains comparable to wild-type embryos (Figure 4A, B, D, E).
evidence: Direct observation from Isl1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 4.

claim: The presence of a tail bud in Isl1 mutants indicates that this gene might not be involved in the activity of the NMC cells.
source: The presence of a tail bud in Isl1 mutants indicates that this gene might not be involved in the activity of the NMC cells, as suggested by its expression pattern (Cai et al., 2003).
evidence: Inference drawn from observation in Isl1 mutants and expression pattern.

claim: In Isl1 mutants, the two layers of the lateral mesoderm, as well as the celomic cavity, extended to the posterior extremity of the embryo.
source: The two layers of the lateral mesoderm, as well as the celomic cavity, extended to the posterior extremity of the embryo (Figure 4H, h', h'').
evidence: Direct observation from Isl1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 4.

claim: Foxf1 expression was upregulated in the posterior of Isl1 mutant embryos, showing a spatial distribution that starts at the dorsal border between the splanchnic and somatic LPM layers, extending to fully cover the somatic lateral mesoderm at more posterior embryonic regions.
source: Foxf1 expression was also upregulated in the posterior of the embryo, showing a spatial distribution that starts at the dorsal border between the splanchnic and somatic LPM layers, extending to fully cover the somatic lateral mesoderm at more posterior embryonic regions (Figure 4h', h'').
evidence: Direct observation from Isl1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 4.

claim: In Isl1 mutants, the DA were expanded into two globular vessels on either side of the gut tube reaching the caudal embryonic end where they merged ventrally.
source: In addition, the DA were expanded into two globular vessels on either side of the gut tube reaching the caudal embryonic end where they merged ventrally (Figure 4h,h', Figure 5C,c,D,d).
evidence: Direct observation from Isl1 mutant embryos shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The connection between umbilical artery and the expanded DAs was highly disorganized in Isl1 mutants.
source: The connection between umbilical artery and the expanded DAs was highly disorganized (Figure 5D).
evidence: Direct observation from Isl1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 5.

claim: Tbx4 was not expressed in the posterior part of Isl1 mutants.
source: Molecular analyses showed that Tbx4 was not expressed in the posterior part of Isl1 mutants (Figure 4I, I', J, J'), indicating that Tbx4 is downstream of Isl1 in the regulatory network controlling the hindlimb/external genitalia, consistent with previous observations using a conditional mutant for Isl1 (Itou et al., 2012; Kawakami et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct observation from Isl1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 4.

claim: Tbx4 is downstream of Isl1 in the regulatory network controlling the hindlimb/external genitalia.
source: Molecular analyses showed that Tbx4 was not expressed in the posterior part of Isl1 mutants (Figure 4I, I', J, J'), indicating that Tbx4 is downstream of Isl1 in the regulatory network controlling the hindlimb/external genitalia, consistent with previous observations using a conditional mutant for Isl1 (Itou et al., 2012; Kawakami et al., 2011).
evidence: Inference drawn from expression analysis in Isl1 mutants and previous studies.

claim: Expression of Foxa2 and Shh at E9.5 showed abnormal morphology at the posterior end of the gut tube in Tgfbr1 mutants.
source: Consistent with this, expression of two endodermal markers, Foxa2 and Shh (Ang et al., 1993; Echelard et al., 1993) at E9.5 showed abnormal morphology at the posterior end of the gut tube (Figure 6A, a, B, b, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 6.

claim: In Tgfbr1−/− embryos, the endodermal tube finished contacting the ventral ectoderm forming a structure reminiscent of the cloacal membrane.
source: This abnormal morphology was clearer in mutant embryos immunostained with the epithelial marker Keratin 8 (Runck et al., 2014), where it was observed that the endodermal tube finished contacting the ventral ectoderm forming a structure reminiscent of the cloacal membrane (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 6.

claim: Tgfbr1−/− embryos lacked the endodermal widening characteristic of the developing cloaca.
source: Also, in contrast with what was observed in wild-type controls, Tgfbr1−/− embryos lacked the endodermal widening characteristic of the developing cloaca and failed to extend the endodermal tube caudal to the cloacal membrane to form the tail gut (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 6.

claim: In wild-type embryos, the tail endodermal tube was strongly positive for Apela.
source: Contrary to wild-type embryos, in which the tail endodermal tube was strongly positive for Apela (Figure 6E, e, F, f), in the Tgfbr1 mutants most of the endodermal tube was negative for this marker, its expression being observed only in a few cells in the dorsal part of the gut tube (Figure 6E', e', F', f').
evidence: Direct observation from wild-type embryos shown in Figure 6.

claim: In Tgfbr1 mutants, most of the endodermal tube was negative for Apela, its expression being observed only in a few cells in the dorsal part of the gut tube.
source: Contrary to wild-type embryos, in which the tail endodermal tube was strongly positive for Apela (Figure 6E, e, F, f), in the Tgfbr1 mutants most of the endodermal tube was negative for this marker, its expression being observed only in a few cells in the dorsal part of the gut tube (Figure 6E', e', F', f').
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 6.

claim: Apela-positive cells were found mixed with the cells of the expanded LPM in Tgfbr1 mutants.
source: Surprisingly, Apela-positive cells were found mixed with the cells of the expanded LPM (Figure 6E', F'), suggesting that endodermal progenitors were produced but misrouted, failing to enter the gut tube.
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 6.

claim: Endodermal progenitors were produced but misrouted in Tgfbr1 mutants, failing to enter the gut tube.
source: Surprisingly, Apela-positive cells were found mixed with the cells of the expanded LPM (Figure 6E', F'), suggesting that endodermal progenitors were produced but misrouted, failing to enter the gut tube.
evidence: Inference drawn from observation of Apela-positive cells in LPM of Tgfbr1 mutants.

claim: Keratin 8 staining was observed scattered within the extended LPM of Tgfbr1 mutant embryos.
source: Consistently with the endodermal origin of the Apela-positive cells, we observed Keratin 8 staining scattered within the extended LPM of the mutant embryos (Figure 6c, d).
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 6.

claim: The visceral endoderm contributes to the formation of the embryonic gut, with the hindgut being particularly populated by this extraembryonic tissue.
source: It has been shown that the visceral endoderm contributes to the formation of the embryonic gut, with the hindgut being particularly populated by this extraembryonic tissue (Kwon et al., 2008).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The dispersal of visceral endodermal cells was not affected by the absence of Tgfbr1 at E7.5.
source: Analysis of E7.5 Afp-GFP+/0:Tgfbr1−/− embryos indicated that the dispersal of visceral endodermal cells was not affected by the absence of Tgfbr1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Afp-GFP-positive visceral endoderm cells were observed in the embryonic endoderm of Tgfbr1 mutant embryos at E8.5, in a distribution comparable to wild-type embryos.
source: In addition, Afp-GFP-positive visceral endoderm cells were observed in the embryonic endoderm of Tgfbr1 mutant embryos at E8.5, in a distribution comparable to wild-type embryos (Figure 7A, A', B, B').
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 7.

claim: At E9.5 and E10.5, the entire endodermal tube of Tgfbr1−/− embryos contained GFP-positive cells.
source: Both at E9.5 and E10.5, the entire endodermal tube of Tgfbr1−/− embryos contained GFP-positive cells, also showing the premature end at the ventral surface of the embryo and the absence of further posterior extension to form the tail gut (Figure 7D–D'', F, F').
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 7.

claim: No Afp-GFP signal was observed mixed with the extended LPM in Tgfbr1 mutants.
source: Importantly, we did not observe Afp-GFP signal mixed with the extended LPM (Figure 7F'', F''').
evidence: Direct observation from Tgfbr1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 7.

claim: The absence of Tgfbr1 does not affect recruitment of visceral endodermal cells to the embryonic gut.
source: These data thus indicate that the absence of Tgfbr1 does not affect recruitment of visceral endodermal cells to the embryonic gut, and that the abnormal Apela patterns observed in Tgfbr1 mutant embryos are unlikely to derive from misrouting of visceral endodermal cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from Afp-GFP reporter analysis in Tgfbr1 mutants.

claim: The abnormal Apela patterns observed in Tgfbr1 mutant embryos are unlikely to derive from misrouting of visceral endodermal cells.
source: These data thus indicate that the absence of Tgfbr1 does not affect recruitment of visceral endodermal cells to the embryonic gut, and that the abnormal Apela patterns observed in Tgfbr1 mutant embryos are unlikely to derive from misrouting of visceral endodermal cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from Afp-GFP reporter analysis in Tgfbr1 mutants.

claim: A significant contribution of Afp-GFP-positive visceral endoderm cells to the embryonic endoderm of wild-type embryos was observed at E8.5.
source: Interestingly, while we observed a significant contribution of Afp-GFP-positive visceral endoderm cells to the embryonic endoderm of wild-type embryos at E8.5 (Figure 7A, A'), we could detect just a few cells in the tail gut of E9.5 embryos (Figure 7C–C'') and virtually none at E10.5 (Figure 7E, E').
evidence: Direct observation from wild-type embryos shown in Figure 7.

claim: Just a few Afp-GFP-positive cells were detected in the tail gut of E9.5 wild-type embryos.
source: Interestingly, while we observed a significant contribution of Afp-GFP-positive visceral endoderm cells to the embryonic endoderm of wild-type embryos at E8.5 (Figure 7A, A'), we could detect just a few cells in the tail gut of E9.5 embryos (Figure 7C–C'') and virtually none at E10.5 (Figure 7E, E').
evidence: Direct observation from wild-type embryos shown in Figure 7.

claim: Virtually no Afp-GFP-positive cells were detected in the tail gut of E10.5 wild-type embryos.
source: Interestingly, while we observed a significant contribution of Afp-GFP-positive visceral endoderm cells to the embryonic endoderm of wild-type embryos at E8.5 (Figure 7A, A'), we could detect just a few cells in the tail gut of E9.5 embryos (Figure 7C–C'') and virtually none at E10.5 (Figure 7E, E').
evidence: Direct observation from wild-type embryos shown in Figure 7.

claim: The visceral endoderm contributes significantly to the embryonic gut up to the region of the cloaca, but is likely to play a minor role in the extension of the endodermal tube growing into the tail.
source: This indicates that, while the visceral endoderm contributes significantly to the embryonic gut up to the region of the cloaca, as previously reported (Kwon et al., 2008), it is likely to play a minor role in the extension of the endodermal tube growing into the tail.
evidence: Inference drawn from Afp-GFP reporter analysis at different stages.

claim: Apela is active in newly generated endodermal tissues, becoming progressively downregulated after they are part of the gut tube.
source: The Apela expression patterns indicate that this gene is active in the newly generated endodermal tissues, becoming progressively downregulated after they are part of the gut tube (Hassan et al., 2010).
evidence: Inference from expression patterns supported by citation.

claim: The tail gut grows from the addition of cells at the tip of this structure.
source: The strong Apela expression restricted to the posterior portion of the endodermal tube within the developing tail (Figure 8A, B, Bb), suggests that the tail gut grows from the addition of cells at the tip of this structure.
evidence: Inference drawn from Apela expression pattern shown in Figure 8.

claim: Analysis of the T-str-creERT:ROSA26-R-gal reporter activity upon tamoxifen administration at E8.0 showed the presence of β-galactosidase-positive cells in the tail gut.
source: Interestingly, analysis of the T-str-creERT:ROSA26-R-gal reporter activity upon tamoxifen administration at E8.0 showed the presence of β-galactosidase-positive cells in the tail gut (Figure 3d).
evidence: Direct observation from lineage tracing experiment shown in Figure 3.

claim: More anterior regions of the gut were negative for β-galactosidase under conditions where labeled cells were present in adjacent mesodermal tissues.
source: Of note, more anterior regions of the gut were negative for β-galactosidase under these conditions, despite the presence of labeled cells in adjacent mesodermal tissues (Figure 3c).
evidence: Direct observation from lineage tracing experiment shown in Figure 3.

claim: The most caudal region of the gut tube grows through the addition of cells generated from a structure derived from the PS located at the end of the growing tail.
source: This suggests that the most caudal region of the gut tube grows through the addition of cells generated from a structure derived from the PS located at the end of the growing tail.
evidence: Hypothesis based on lineage tracing and expression data.

claim: An Apela-positive structure was observed adjacent to the tip of the gut at the posterior end of the growing tail.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we observed an Apela-positive structure adjacent to the tip of the gut at the posterior end of the growing tail (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: DiI-mediated cell tracing showed that DiI-positive cells were observed in the gut tube epithelium after 20 hr in culture.
source: We further tested whether this Apela- and Keratin 8-positive region at the tip of the tail bud contributes to the gut tube using a DiI-mediated cell tracing approach ex vivo. E9.5 embryos injected with DiI that showed no label in the gut tube just after injection (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A-c3) were analyzed after 20 hr in culture (Figure 8E–h', Figure 8—figure supplement 2). In the three embryos that filled this criterium, DiI-positive cells were observed in the gut tube epithelium.
evidence: Direct observation from DiI tracing experiment shown in Figure 8.

claim: The presence of DiI signal in the gut epithelium supports the existence of a region at the tip of the tail bud able to generate cells that become incorporated into the tail gut.
source: Even considering the possible leakage of the DiI into the NMC compartment, the presence of DiI signal in the gut epithelium further supports the existence of a region at the tip of the tail bud able to generate cells that become incorporated into the tail gut.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from DiI tracing experiment.

claim: Formation of spinal cord and somitic mesoderm is maintained by the relocation of the neural-mesodermal-competent cells from the caudal lateral epiblast in the epiblast into the CNH in the tail bud through an incomplete EMT triggered by the concurrent activity of Tgfbr1 and Snai1.
source: Formation of spinal cord and somitic mesoderm is maintained by the relocation of the neural-mesodermal-competent cells from the caudal lateral epiblast CLE in the epiblast into the CNH in the tail bud through an incomplete EMT triggered by the concurrent activity of Tgfbr1 and Snai1 (Cambray and Wilson, 2007; Dias et al., 2020; Henrique et al., 2015; Wilson et al., 2009; Wymeersch et al., 2021; Wymeersch et al., 2019).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The progenitors of the lateral mesoderm undergo a process of terminal differentiation resulting in the formation of the primordia of the hindlimb and of the external genitalia.
source: The progenitors of the lateral mesoderm, however, undergo a process of terminal differentiation resulting in the formation of the primordia of the hindlimb and of the external genitalia (Jurberg et al., 2013).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Tgfbr1 signaling is both necessary and sufficient to activate the mechanisms regulating terminal differentiation processes in the lateral mesoderm.
source: Genetic analyses indicate that Tgfbr1 signaling is both necessary and sufficient to activate the mechanisms regulating those terminal differentiation processes, as illustrated by their premature activation in transgenic gain of function experiments (Jurberg et al., 2013) and the absence of early markers for the primordia of the hindlimb or the GT in Tgfbr1 null mutant embryos (Dias et al., 2020).
evidence: Conclusion from genetic analyses supported by citations.

claim: The requirement of Tgfbr1 encompasses the development of many tissues undergoing morphological and functional reorganization during the trunk to tail transition, including the major vascular system and the embryonic endoderm.
source: Our data now show that the requirement of Tgfbr1 encompasses the development of many other tissues undergoing a morphological and functional reorganization during the trunk to tail transition, including the major vascular system and the embryonic endoderm.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the current study's findings.

claim: The posterior PS/allantois is a candidate for the structure mediating the different Tgfbr1-dependent processes involving the lateral mesoderm and endoderm during the trunk to tail transition.
source: An interesting conclusion from our work is the identification of the posterior PS/allantois as a candidate for the structure mediating the different Tgfbr1-dependent processes involving the lateral mesoderm and endoderm during the trunk to tail transition.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the current study's findings.

claim: Cell tracing experiments identified the posterior epiblast/PS as the region providing the cells building the trunk LPM.
source: Cell tracing experiments identified the posterior epiblast/PS as the region providing the cells building the trunk LPM (Wymeersch et al., 2016), being the posterior PS abutting the allantois also involved in organizing the recruitment of visceral endodermal cells to the embryonic gut tube (Rodriguez and Downs, 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The posterior PS abutting the allantois is involved in organizing the recruitment of visceral endodermal cells to the embryonic gut tube.
source: Cell tracing experiments identified the posterior epiblast/PS as the region providing the cells building the trunk LPM (Wymeersch et al., 2016), being the posterior PS abutting the allantois also involved in organizing the recruitment of visceral endodermal cells to the embryonic gut tube (Rodriguez and Downs, 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The transition to tail development entails the fading of the epiblast and PS, as they become replaced by the tail bud as the main driver of axial extension.
source: The transition to tail development entails the fading of the epiblast and PS, as they become replaced by the tail bud as the main driver of axial extension.
evidence: Established developmental process.

claim: At the trunk to tail transition stage, the allantois leaves its position at the posterior end of the embryo to occupy more anterior and ventral positions while organizing the connection between embryonic and extraembryonic structures.
source: At this stage, the allantois also leaves its position at the posterior end of the embryo to occupy more anterior and ventral positions while organizing the connection between embryonic and extraembryonic structures (Arora and Papaioannou, 2012; Downs and Rodriguez, 2020).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Genes involved in vascular morphogenesis are specifically expressed in the posterior epiblast/PS region.
source: Gene expression analysis shows that genes involved in vascular morphogenesis are specifically expressed in the posterior epiblast/PS region (Wymeersch et al., 2019).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The posterior epiblast/PS generates the VLM posterior to the allantois during the trunk to tail transition.
source: Cell tracing experiments indicate that the posterior epiblast/PS, which lays down the LPM during trunk formation, generates the VLM posterior to the allantois during the trunk to tail transition (Wymeersch et al., 2016) and that these cells contribute to the primordium of the external genitalia later in development (Tschopp et al., 2014).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cells from the posterior epiblast/PS contribute to the primordium of the external genitalia later in development.
source: Cell tracing experiments indicate that the posterior epiblast/PS, which lays down the LPM during trunk formation, generates the VLM posterior to the allantois during the trunk to tail transition (Wymeersch et al., 2016) and that these cells contribute to the primordium of the external genitalia later in development (Tschopp et al., 2014).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The absence of VLM in the Tgfbr1 mutants indicates that signaling through this receptor is required to organize the proper switch of the posterior epiblast/PS from a trunk developmental mode, involving entering VLM fates.
source: The absence of VLM in the Tgfbr1 mutants indicates that signaling through this receptor is required to organize the proper switch of the posterior epiblast/PS from a trunk developmental mode, involving entering VLM fates.
evidence: Inference drawn from observations in Tgfbr1 mutants.

claim: Foxf1 is expressed in the posterior PS and maintains expression in the derivatives of this structure after the transition to tail development.
source: Foxf1, which is expressed in the posterior PS, maintains expression in the derivatives of this structure after the transition to tail development (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Astorga and Carlsson, 2007).
evidence: Observation supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citation.

claim: The strong and expanded Foxf1 expression throughout the posterior end of the extended LPM of the Tgfbr1 mutant embryos represents a molecular vestige of posterior PS that failed to form the VLM.
source: We suggest that the strong and expanded Foxf1 expression throughout the posterior end of the extended LPM of the Tgfbr1 mutant embryos represents a molecular vestige of posterior PS that failed to form the VLM, and instead became trapped within mis-patterned LPM extending from the trunk.
evidence: Hypothesis based on observations in Tgfbr1 mutants.

claim: The posterior PS is thought to play a relevant role in the connection of the paired DAs with the allantois artery to link the embryonic and extraembryonic vascular systems.
source: As the posterior PS is also thought to play a relevant role in the connection of the paired DAs with the allantois artery to link the embryonic and extraembryonic vascular systems (Downs and Rodriguez, 2020), defective posterior PS reorganization during the trunk to tail transition could explain the DA abnormalities observed in the Tgfbr1 mutant embryos.
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: Defective posterior PS reorganization during the trunk to tail transition could explain the DA abnormalities observed in the Tgfbr1 mutant embryos.
source: As the posterior PS is also thought to play a relevant role in the connection of the paired DAs with the allantois artery to link the embryonic and extraembryonic vascular systems (Downs and Rodriguez, 2020), defective posterior PS reorganization during the trunk to tail transition could explain the DA abnormalities observed in the Tgfbr1 mutant embryos.
evidence: Hypothesis based on observations in Tgfbr1 mutants and previous knowledge.

claim: Signaling through Tgfbr1 is essential for the development of the endodermal tube posterior to the cloacal plate and potentially the cloaca itself.
source: Analysis of Tgfbr1−/− embryos revealed that signaling through this receptor is essential for the development of the endodermal tube posterior to the cloacal plate and potentially the cloaca itself.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from analysis of Tgfbr1 mutants.

claim: The low levels of Apela expression in the endoderm of the Tgfbr1 mutants might indicate that this structure was generated earlier in development, during the phase of trunk extension.
source: The low levels of Apela expression in the endoderm of the Tgfbr1 mutants might thus indicate that this structure was generated earlier in development, during the phase of trunk extension.
evidence: Hypothesis based on Apela expression patterns in Tgfbr1 mutants.

claim: The presence of Apela signal mixed with the LPM suggests that new endodermal cells are still produced but failed to enter the gut, being instead mistargeted to the mesoderm.
source: In addition, the presence of Apela signal mixed with the LPM suggests that new endodermal cells are still produced but failed to enter the gut, being instead mistargeted to the mesoderm.
evidence: Inference drawn from Apela expression patterns in Tgfbr1 mutants.

claim: The similarities between the Apela and Foxf1 expression in the posterior region of Tgfbr1 mutant embryos suggest that their developmental history might be somehow linked.
source: Interestingly, the similarities between the Apela and Foxf1 expression in the posterior region of Tgfbr1 mutant embryos suggest that their developmental history might be somehow linked.
evidence: Hypothesis based on expression pattern similarities in Tgfbr1 mutants.

claim: Tail gut growth is organized by a structure derived from a specific region of the posterior PS that enters the tail during the transition to tail development.
source: Given the role of the posterior PS abutting the allantois in the recruitment of visceral endodermal cells to the embryonic gut (Rodriguez and Downs, 2017), it is possible that tail gut growth is organized by a structure derived from a specific region of the posterior PS that enters the tail during the transition to tail development.
evidence: Hypothesis based on previous knowledge and current observations.

claim: The observation that the ROSA26 reporter labels the tail gut when activated by the T-str-creERT driver at the stage of the trunk to tail transition is consistent with the involvement of the PS or a derivative of this structure in the formation of the gut tube posterior to the cloacal membrane.
source: In addition, the observation that the ROSA26 reporter labels the tail gut when activated by the T-str-creERT driver at the stage of the trunk to tail transition (Anderson et al., 2013; Figure 3d) is consistent with the involvement of the PS or a derivative of this structure in the formation of the gut tube posterior to the cloacal membrane.
evidence: Inference drawn from lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3 and cited study.

claim: The transition of the PS-derived structure contributing to tail gut formation should be under Tgfbr1 control.
source: Were this the case, the transition of this PS-derived structure should be under Tgfbr1 control.
evidence: Logical inference from the hypothesis about PS involvement in tail gut formation.

claim: The control of the trunk to tail transition by Tgfbr1 entails two distinct, and apparently independent, components acting on two areas of the epiblast/PS.
source: Taken together, this work along with previous studies, suggests that the control of the trunk to tail transition by Tgfbr1 entails two distinct, and apparently independent, components acting on two areas of the epiblast/PS.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the current study and previous work.

claim: The first component of Tgfbr1 control involves a cooperation between Tgfbr1 and Snai1 to organize the relocation of NMC progenitors from the CLE to the CNH through a partial EMT.
source: The first component involves a cooperation between Tgfbr1 and Snai1 to organize the relocation of NMC progenitors from the CLE to the CNH through a partial EMT (Dias et al., 2020).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The first component of Tgfbr1 control is associated with the generation of the tail bud that replaces the epiblast/PS as the driver of axial elongation.
source: This component is also associated with the generation of the tail bud that replaces the epiblast/PS as the driver of axial elongation (Wilson et al., 2009; Wymeersch et al., 2021).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The second component of Tgfbr1 control targets the posterior part of the epiblast/PS containing the progenitors for the lateral mesoderm as well as an organizing center for endodermal development.
source: The second component would target the posterior part of the epiblast/PS containing the progenitors for the lateral mesoderm as well as an organizing center for endodermal development (summarized in Figure 9).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the current study summarized in Figure 9.

claim: Tgfbr1 activity triggers a combination of programs leading to the organization of the exit channels of the intestinal and urogenital systems, the connection of the embryonic and extraembryonic circulation, and the formation of the hindlimbs and external genitalia.
source: Here, Tgfbr1 activity triggers a combination of programs leading to the organization of the exit channels of the intestinal and urogenital systems, as well as the connection of the embryonic and extraembryonic circulation, and the formation of the hindlimbs and external genitalia.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the current study's findings.

claim: The finding that Isl1 mutants exhibit many of the features observed in the lateral mesoderm and vascular system of Tgfbr1 mutants, together with the absence of Isl1 expression in Tgfbr1 mutants, identifies Isl1 as a key downstream mediator of the second component of Tgfbr1 activity controlling the trunk to tail transition.
source: The finding that Isl1 mutants exhibit many of the features observed in the lateral mesoderm and vascular system of Tgfbr1 mutants, together with the absence of Isl1 expression in Tgfbr1 mutants (Dias et al., 2020) identifies Isl1 as a key downstream mediator of the second component of Tgfbr1 activity controlling the trunk to tail transition.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of Isl1 and Tgfbr1 mutant phenotypes.
